title: Subject pronouns and essere
summary: I, you, he… and the verb “to be”.

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: Italian has one subject pronoun for each person. The verb changes for every person, so the pronoun is usually left out: *sono italiano* already means “I am Italian”. Use the pronoun only for emphasis or contrast.
*Lei* (with a capital L) is the polite “you”. It takes the same verb form as *lei* (she): *Lei è italiano?* = “Are you Italian?”.
*Essere* (to be) is irregular — learn it by heart:
*è* (is) has an accent. Without it, *e* means “and”.

exercises.why: Third person singular is *è* — with the accent. *e* means “and”.

exercises.en: Marco and Anna are in Rome.
exercises.why: Two people = *loro* → *sono*. Note that *io* and *loro* share the form *sono*.

exercises.en: Which pronoun is the polite “you” (one person)?
exercises.why: *Lei* is the formal “you” and uses the third-person verb: *Lei è…*.

title: Avere – to have
summary: The verb “to have” and its everyday expressions.

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: *Avere* (to have) is the second key irregular verb. It is also used to build past tenses later on.
The *h* in *ho, hai, ha, hanno* is silent. It only tells them apart from *o* (or), *ai* (to the), *a* (to) and *anno* (year).
Italian uses *avere* where English uses “to be” for age and for many feelings:

exercises.en: How do you say “I am cold”?
My brother is ten years old.

title: Nouns: gender and plural
summary: Masculine or feminine, one or many.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Italian grammar: Inflection of nouns
FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: Every Italian noun is masculine or feminine. The ending usually tells you which, and it changes in the plural.
Nouns ending in *-e* can be either gender — learn them with their article: *il fiore* (m), *la chiave* (f).
Some nouns never change in the plural: nouns ending in a stressed vowel (*la città → le città*, *il caffè → i caffè*) and foreign words (*il film → i film*, *il bar → i bar*).
Spelling: nouns in *-ca / -ga* add an *h* to keep the hard sound: *amica → amiche*. Nouns in *-co / -go* vary: *gioco → giochi*, *lago → laghi*, but *amico → amici*, *medico → medici*.
A few common nouns are irregular: *uomo → uomini*, *uovo → uova* (feminine in the plural), *mano → mani* (feminine, though it ends in *-o*).

exercises.why: Nouns in *-e* → *-i* in the plural, whatever their gender.
Nouns ending in a stressed vowel do not change.
*la mano* is feminine even though it ends in *-o*. Plural: *le mani*.
Foreign words do not change in the plural.

title: The definite article (the)
summary: *il, lo, l’, la, i, gli, le*

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: “The” has seven forms. The choice depends on gender, number and the first sound of the next word.

head: Singular
Plural
Used before
rows: s + consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y: *lo studente → gli studenti*, *lo zio → gli zii*

blocks.text: Italian uses the article more than English does — also with general ideas and likes: *Il caffè è buono* (Coffee is good), *Amo la musica* (I love music).
The article goes with the word right after it, not with the noun: *lo zaino*, but *il grande zaino*. And *gli* is the plural of both *lo* and *l’*.

exercises.why: Masculine, starts with a normal consonant → *il*.

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: “A / an” follows the same sound rules as “the”:

head: Form
Used before
Example
rows: s + consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y

blocks.text: Only the feminine takes an apostrophe: *un amico* (m) but *un’amica* (f). That apostrophe tells you the gender in writing.
There is no plural “a”. For “some” use *dei, degli, delle* (see the lesson on partitives) or nothing at all: *Ho amici a Roma*.

items.en: I am looking for a pharmacy.

exercises.why: Feminine before a vowel → *un’* with the apostrophe.
Masculine before a vowel → *un*, no apostrophe.
*ora* is feminine and starts with a vowel → *un’ora*.

exercises.sentence: Ho una sorella e un fratello
exercises.en: I have a sister and a brother.
exercises.why: *una* for the feminine noun, *un* for the masculine one.

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: Adjectives agree with their noun in gender and number. There are two main types:

items.it: il vestito rosso, la gonna rossa
items.en: the red dress, the red skirt

items.it: i vestiti rossi, le gonne rosse
items.en: the red dresses, the red skirts

items.it: un libro interessante, una storia interessante
items.en: an interesting book, an interesting story

blocks.text: Position: most adjectives come after the noun (colours, nationalities, shapes): *una macchina nera*, *un ragazzo italiano*. A few very common ones usually come before: *bello, buono, grande, piccolo, nuovo, vecchio*: *una bella casa*, *un piccolo problema*.
If a group mixes masculine and feminine, the adjective is masculine plural: *Marco e Anna sono simpatici*.

exercises.why: *felice* is an *-e* adjective: plural *felici* for both genders.

exercises.en: Which is the natural word order?
exercises.why: Colours come after the noun, and agree: *macchina nera*.

exercises.en: I have a nice new house.
exercises.why: *bella* before the noun is common; *nuova* here comes after.

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: Verbs are grouped by their infinitive ending: *-are*, *-ere*, *-ire*. The *-are* group is the largest. To conjugate, remove *-are* and add the endings *-o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano*.
The present tense covers English “I speak”, “I am speaking” and often “I will speak”: *Domani parto* = “I’m leaving tomorrow”.
Verbs in *-care / -gare* add *h* before *i*: *cercare → cerchi, cerchiamo*; *pagare → paghi, paghiamo*. Verbs in *-iare* keep only one *i*: *mangiare → mangi, mangiamo*.

exercises.en: They are waiting for the train.
Are you looking for the keys?
exercises.why: *-care* verbs add *h* to keep the hard sound: *cerchi*.

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: *-ere* and *-ire* verbs share most endings: *-o, -i, -e, -iamo*. Only *voi* differs (*-ete* / *-ite*), and *loro* ends in *-ono*.
Many *-ire* verbs add *-isc-* in every form except *noi* and *voi*. Common ones: *capire, finire, preferire, pulire, spedire*.
There is no rule to tell *dormire*-type from *capire*-type verbs: check the dictionary. Most new *-ire* verbs are the *-isc-* type.

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: The most frequent verbs are irregular in the present. These come up in almost every conversation:

*stare* means “to be / to stay”, used for health and in fixed phrases: *Come stai?* (How are you?), *Sto bene* (I’m well). *fare* is used for weather and many activities: *Fa freddo* (It’s cold), *fare la spesa* (to do the shopping).

exercises.en: Are you coming to the party?

exercises.why: *uscire* → *esc-* only in *io, tu, lui, loro*; *voi uscite*.

blocks.text: *dovere* (must, to have to), *potere* (can, may) and *volere* (to want) are followed directly by an infinitive, with no preposition: *Devo lavorare* (I have to work).
Polite requests often use *potere*: *Può ripetere?* (Can you repeat?). For “I would like” use *vorrei* — a form of *volere* you will meet later (conditional).

items.en: I have to leave at six.

exercises.en: Do you want an ice cream?
Which is correct for “I want to eat”?
exercises.why: Modal verb + plain infinitive, no preposition.

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: To make a sentence negative, put *non* right before the verb: *Parlo tedesco → Non parlo tedesco*.

Words like *niente* (nothing), *nessuno* (nobody) and *mai* (never) go after the verb, and *non* stays: *Non vedo niente* (I don’t see anything), *Non viene mai* (He never comes). This double negative is correct in Italian.
Questions use the same word order as statements; only the intonation (and the question mark) changes: *Parli italiano?* = Do you speak Italian?
Before *è*, *dove* and *come* usually lose their last letter: *Dov’è la stazione?* *Com’è?*

exercises.en: I never go to the cinema.

title: Simple prepositions
summary: *di, a, da, in, con, su, per, tra / fra*

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

head: Preposition
Main meanings
Example
rows: *Vengo da Napoli*, *Studio da un anno*, *dal medico*

blocks.text: Cities take *a*, countries and regions take *in*: *a Firenze*, *in Toscana*, *in Italia*. Means of transport take *in*: *in macchina, in treno, in aereo* — but *a piedi* (on foot).
*da* + time = how long something has been going on, with the present tense: *Abito qui da due anni* = I have been living here for two years.

exercises.en: I go to work by car.
I have been studying Italian for six months.

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: When *di, a, da, in, su* come before a definite article, they merge with it into one word:
*in* changes to *ne-*, and all forms with *lo, la, le, l’* double the *l*. *con, per, tra, fra* do not merge in modern Italian: *con il*, *per la*.

items.en: The book is on the table.
I’m coming back from the office.
The keys are in the bag.

exercises.en: The cat is on the sofa.
The milk is in the fridge.
I come back from the office at six.

exercises.it: Ci sono molti turisti ___ città. (in + le)
exercises.en: There are many tourists in the cities.
Which preposition does NOT merge with the article in modern Italian?

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: “There is” = *c’è* (*ci* + *è*). “There are” = *ci sono*. The verb agrees with what comes after it.

items.it: Ci sono due bar qui vicino.
items.en: There are two bars near here.

blocks.text: Questions just add the question mark: *C’è un bagno?* (Is there a bathroom?). *Ecco* (here is / here are) is used to point something out: *Ecco il treno!*

exercises.en: There is a pharmacy near here.

exercises.sentence: Ci sono tre libri sul tavolo
exercises.en: There are three books on the table.

title: Possessives
summary: *mio, tuo, suo*… and when to drop the article

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: Possessives agree with the thing owned, not with the owner: *la sua casa* = his house or her house (*casa* is feminine).
The possessive normally has the article in front: *il mio libro*, *la nostra casa*, *i tuoi amici*.

Exception: no article with a single family member — *mia madre*, *tuo fratello*, *sua sorella*. The article comes back in the plural (*le mie sorelle*), with *loro* (*la loro madre*), and when the noun is modified (*la mia sorella minore*). *mamma* and *papà* usually keep it: *la mia mamma*.

exercises.why: Normal nouns keep the article: *il mio libro*.
Single family member → no article: *mia madre*.
Plural family members take the article: *i miei fratelli*.
*moglie* is feminine → *sua*; single family member → no article.
Agreement is with *fratello* (masculine), not with Anna: *suo fratello*.

exercises.sentence: Questa è la mia amica Giulia
exercises.why: *amica* is not a family member, so it keeps the article.

blocks.text: *questo* (this) is a regular adjective: *questo, questa, questi, queste*. Before a vowel in the singular it can become *quest’*: *quest’anno*.
*quello* (that), before a noun, changes like the definite article:
Used alone as a pronoun, it is simply *quello, quella, quelli, quelle*: *Preferisco quello* (I prefer that one).

items.en: This year I’m going to Sicily.

exercises.en: Do you want this bag or that one?

blocks.text: Reflexive verbs end in *-arsi, -ersi, -irsi* in the infinitive. The action falls back on the subject, so a reflexive pronoun goes before the verb:

Many daily-routine verbs are reflexive in Italian: *svegliarsi* (to wake up), *lavarsi* (to wash), *vestirsi* (to get dressed), *divertirsi* (to have fun), *sentirsi* (to feel), *sposarsi* (to get married).
With an infinitive, the pronoun can attach to it: *Devo alzarmi presto* = *Mi devo alzare presto*.
In the past tense reflexive verbs always use *essere*: *Mi sono alzato alle sette*.

items.en: We have a lot of fun.

exercises.en: We have fun at the party.
They are getting married in June.
Tomorrow I have to get up early.
exercises.why: Pronoun attached to the infinitive must match the subject: *io* → *alzarmi*.
Each reflexive verb takes its own pronoun.

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: The *passato prossimo* is the main past tense of spoken Italian. It translates both “I spoke” and “I have spoken”. Form: present of *avere* (or *essere*) + past participle.
Most verbs — all verbs that take a direct object — use *avere*. With *avere* the participle does not change for the subject: *Anna ha mangiato*, *i ragazzi hanno mangiato*.
Many common participles are irregular:

exercises.why: *fare* → *fatto*; with *avere* no agreement with the subject.

exercises.sentence: Abbiamo preso il treno delle otto
exercises.en: We took the eight o’clock train.

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: Some verbs build the *passato prossimo* with *essere*. These are mainly verbs of movement and change of state with no direct object, plus all reflexive verbs:
With *essere* the participle agrees with the subject like an adjective: *-o, -a, -i, -e*.
Reflexive verbs also take *essere* and agree: *Anna si è alzata*, *ci siamo divertiti*.

exercises.en: Guys, what time did you get up?
Which verb takes *avere* in the passato prossimo?

title: Direct object pronouns
summary: *mi, ti, lo, la, ci, vi, li, le*

blocks.text: Direct object pronouns replace the object of the verb (“it”, “him”, “them”) and go right before the conjugated verb.

items.en: Do you know Marco? – Yes, I know him.

items.it: Dove sono le chiavi? Non le trovo.
items.en: Where are the keys? I can’t find them.

items.it: Prendi il caffè? – Sì, lo prendo.
items.en: Will you have the coffee? – Yes, I’ll have it.

blocks.text: In the *passato prossimo*, *lo* and *la* become *l’* before *ho, hai, ha, hanno*, and the participle agrees with *lo, la, li, le*: *Hai visto Anna? – Sì, l’ho vista.* *Hai comprato le mele? – Sì, le ho comprate.*
With an infinitive the pronoun can attach to it: *Voglio vederlo* = *Lo voglio vedere*.

exercises.en: Are you buying the newspaper? – Yes, I’m buying it.
Do you see Giulia? – Yes, I see her.

exercises.it: Inviti i tuoi amici? – Sì, ___ invito.
exercises.en: Are you inviting your friends? – Yes, I’m inviting them.

exercises.it: Mangi le fragole? – No, non ___ mangio.
exercises.en: Do you eat strawberries? – No, I don’t eat them.
Did you see Anna? – Yes, I saw her.

exercises.it: Hai comprato i biglietti? – Sì, li ho ___.
exercises.en: Did you buy the tickets? – Yes, I bought them.
Will you help me? – Yes, I’ll help you.
I don’t want to see him.
exercises.why: Pronoun before the conjugated verb (or attached: *Non voglio vederlo*).

blocks.text: Indirect object pronouns mean “to me”, “to him”… They go before the verb.
“To them” is *gli* in everyday Italian; formal written Italian uses *loro* after the verb: *Do loro un regalo*.
*piacere* (to like) works backwards: the thing you like is the subject. Literally *Mi piace il caffè* = “Coffee pleases me”. Use *piace* with one thing or a verb, *piacciono* with several things.
In the past, *piacere* takes *essere* and agrees with the thing liked: *Mi è piaciuta la pizza*.

exercises.it: Telefono a Maria e ___ dico la verità.
exercises.en: I call Maria and tell her the truth.
We like the present a lot.

exercises.why: *piacere* uses *essere* in the past: *ti è piaciuta*.

blocks.text: The *imperfetto* describes the past as it was going on: habits (“I used to”), descriptions, and actions in progress (“I was doing”). It is very regular: take the infinitive, remove *-re*, add *-vo, -vi, -va, -vamo, -vate, -vano*.
Only a few verbs are irregular. The most important is *essere*:
*fare* (*facevo*), *dire* (*dicevo*) and *bere* (*bevevo*) use their old, longer stems.

items.en: As a child I used to play football.
While I was reading, he was sleeping.
We used to have a dog.

exercises.it: Da piccolo ___ al mare ogni estate. (andare, io)
exercises.en: As a child I used to go to the seaside every summer.
When you were young, did you use to read a lot?
We always used to do our homework.
Did you use to live in the countryside?
The children were playing in the garden.
While I was cooking, I was listening to the radio.
exercises.why: Two actions in progress at the same time → both in the *imperfetto*.

blocks.text: Both are past tenses, but they show the past differently:

head: passato prossimo
imperfetto
rows: a completed event, a single action: *Ieri ho visto Marco.*
a sequence of events: *Sono entrato, ho salutato e mi sono seduto.*
a description (weather, age, feelings, time): *Faceva freddo. Avevo dieci anni.*
an action with a set length: *Ho dormito otto ore.*

blocks.text: They often appear together: the *imperfetto* sets the scene, the *passato prossimo* reports what happened: *Mentre camminavo, ho incontrato Anna* = While I was walking, I met Anna.
Signal words — *ogni giorno, sempre, di solito, mentre* → usually *imperfetto*; *ieri, una volta, all’improvviso, alle tre* → usually *passato prossimo*.

items.it: Quando ero piccolo, andavo a scuola a piedi.
items.en: When I was small I used to walk to school.

items.it: Ieri sono andato a scuola in autobus.
items.en: Yesterday I went to school by bus.

items.it: Pioveva, quindi sono rimasto a casa.
items.en: It was raining, so I stayed at home.

exercises.en: Yesterday I saw a good film.
As a girl I always used to drink milk.

exercises.it: Mentre ___ la doccia, è suonato il telefono.
exercises.en: While I was having a shower, the phone rang.
exercises.why: Action in progress → *imperfetto*; the interruption → *passato prossimo*.

exercises.en: While I was watching TV, Marco arrived.
exercises.why: The event that interrupts → *passato prossimo*, with *essere*.

exercises.it: Quando ___ dieci anni, abitavo a Napoli.
exercises.en: When I was ten, I lived in Naples.
Last Saturday we danced until midnight.
exercises.why: A finished event with a clear end → *passato prossimo*.

exercises.sentence: Era tardi e non c’era nessuno
exercises.en: It was late and there was nobody there.

blocks.text: The *futuro semplice* is formed from the infinitive without the final *-e*; *-are* verbs change *a* to *e*. Endings: *-ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno*.
Common irregular futures shorten or change the stem:
Others: *potere → potrò*, *dovere → dovrò*, *vedere → vedrò*, *sapere → saprò*, *venire → verrò*, *volere → vorrò*, *bere → berrò*, *rimanere → rimarrò*, *stare → starò*, *dare → darò*.
The future also expresses a guess about the present: *Che ore sono? – Saranno le tre* = It’s probably three.

items.en: Next year we’ll go to Greece.

exercises.en: The train will arrive at three.
We’ll go to Rome in summer.
They will be tired after the trip.
I don’t know if I’ll be able to come.
The weather will be nice tomorrow.

title: Some: the partitive
summary: *del, della, dei, delle, un po’ di*

sources.name: FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: “Some / any” is expressed with *di* + definite article (the same merged forms as in the prepositions lesson):

items.it: Ci sono degli studenti in classe.
items.en: There are some students in the classroom.

blocks.text: Alternatives: *un po’ di* (a bit of) with things you can’t count, *alcuni / alcune* (a few) with plurals: *un po’ di zucchero*, *alcuni amici*.
In negative sentences the partitive is usually dropped: *Non ho pane* (I don’t have any bread).

exercises.en: Do you put a bit of sugar in your coffee?

exercises.why: In negative sentences the partitive is normally dropped.

exercises.sentence: Ho comprato del pane e delle uova
exercises.en: I bought some bread and some eggs.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Italian grammar: Pronouns (ci, vi, ne)

blocks.text: *ci* replaces a place introduced by *a, in, su*, or a phrase with *a*: *Vai a Roma? – Sì, ci vado domani* (Yes, I’m going there tomorrow). *Pensi al lavoro? – Sì, ci penso* (Yes, I think about it).
*ne* replaces a quantity or a phrase with *di*: *Quanti figli hai? – Ne ho due* (I have two [of them]). *Parli del film? – Sì, ne parlo* (Yes, I’m talking about it).
With a number or quantity word, *ne* is required — Italian can’t just say “I have two”: *Ne ho due*, *Ne voglio un po’*, *Non ne ho*.
*ci* + *è / sono* → *c’è*, *ci sono*: the same *ci* means “there”.

exercises.en: Are you coming to the cinema? – Yes, I’m coming.
How many brothers do you have? – I have two.

exercises.it: Hai del pane? – No, non ___ ho.
exercises.en: Do you have any bread? – No, I don’t have any.

exercises.it: Pensi spesso alle vacanze? – Sì, ___ penso sempre.
exercises.en: Do you often think about the holidays? – Yes, I always think about them.

exercises.it: Che ne pensi del libro? – ___ penso bene.
exercises.en: What do you think of the book? – I think well of it.

exercises.it: Abiti a Milano? – Sì, ___ abito da tre anni.
exercises.en: Do you live in Milan? – Yes, I’ve lived there for three years.

exercises.it: Quanti caffè bevi? – ___ bevo due al giorno.
exercises.en: How many coffees do you drink? – I drink two a day.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Italian grammar: Combinations of clitics

blocks.text: When an indirect pronoun (to me, to you…) and a direct pronoun (it, them) go together, the indirect comes first and *mi, ti, ci, vi* change their *i* to *e*. *gli* and *le* both become *glie-* and join the direct pronoun into one word.

items.it: Mi presti la penna? – Sì, te la presto.
items.en: Will you lend me the pen? – Yes, I’ll lend it to you.

items.it: Hai dato il libro a Marco? – Sì, gliel’ho dato.
items.en: Did you give Marco the book? – Yes, I gave it to him.

items.it: Ci porti i documenti? – Ve li porto domani.
items.en: Will you bring us the documents? – I’ll bring them to you tomorrow.

blocks.text: *glielo* means “it to him”, “it to her” and “it to you (Lei)” — context tells which.

exercises.it: Mi dai il numero? – Sì, ___ do.
exercises.en: Will you give me the number? – Yes, I’ll give it to you.

exercises.it: Regali i fiori a Anna? – Sì, ___ regalo.
exercises.en: Are you giving the flowers to Anna? – Yes, I’m giving them to her.

exercises.it: Ci mandi la foto? – Sì, ___ mando.
exercises.en: Will you send us the photo? – Yes, I’ll send it to you.

exercises.it: Chi ti ha detto la notizia? – ___ ha detta Marco.
exercises.en: Who told you the news? – Marco told me.

exercises.it: Hai spiegato la regola agli studenti? – Sì, ___ ho spiegata.
exercises.en: Did you explain the rule to the students? – Yes, I explained it to them.

exercises.it: Quante pizze ci porti? – ___ porto tre.
exercises.en: How many pizzas are you bringing us? – I’m bringing you three.

exercises.it: Puoi prestare la macchina a tuo fratello? – Sì, posso ___.
exercises.en: Can you lend your car to your brother? – Yes, I can lend it to him.

blocks.text: The *condizionale presente* uses the same stem as the future, with the endings *-ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero*.

Verbs with irregular future stems use the same stem here: *essere → sarei*, *avere → avrei*, *andare → andrei*, *potere → potrei*, *dovere → dovrei*, *volere → vorrei*, *venire → verrei*, *fare → farei*.

Uses: polite requests (*Vorrei un caffè*, *Potrebbe aiutarmi?*), wishes (*Mi piacerebbe viaggiare*), advice with *dovere* (*Dovresti riposare* = You should rest), and what would happen (*Io andrei, ma piove*).
*noi* forms: future *parleremo* (one m) vs conditional *parleremmo* (double m). The difference matters!

exercises.it: Noi ___ volentieri, ma non abbiamo tempo. (venire)
exercises.en: We’d gladly come, but we don’t have time.
I would like to live by the sea.

exercises.it: Voi che cosa ___ al mio posto? (fare)
exercises.en: What would you do in my place?
They would be happy to see you.

exercises.why: Polite request with the conditional of *potere*.

blocks.text: The imperative gives orders and instructions. *tu*, *noi* and *voi* forms are the real imperative; *Lei* and *Loro* borrow the present subjunctive.
Note *tu parla!* (not *parli*) for *-are* verbs. Common irregular *tu* forms: *va’ / vai* (go), *fa’ / fai* (do), *da’ / dai* (give), *sta’ / stai* (stay), *di’* (say), *sii* (be), *abbi* (have).
Negative *tu* = *non* + infinitive: *Non parlare!* (Don’t speak!). Other persons just add *non*: *Non parlate!*
Pronouns attach to the end of *tu, noi, voi* forms: *Prendilo!* (Take it!), *Diciamolo!*, *Scrivetemi!*. With *Lei* they go before: *Mi dica* (Tell me).
The short forms *va’, fa’, da’, di’, sta’* double the first consonant of an attached pronoun: *dimmi* (tell me), *fallo* (do it), *dammi* (give me).

exercises.it: Questo libro è bello: ___! (leggere + lo, tu)
exercises.en: This book is good: read it!

sources.name: Wikipedia – Italian grammar: Degrees of comparison
Wikibooks – Italian grammar: Comparatives and superlatives
FSI Italian FAST – Language-usage notes & Appendix A

blocks.text: Comparisons use *più* (more) and *meno* (less). “Than” is *di* before nouns and pronouns, *che* before adjectives, verbs, and phrases with a preposition.

items.it: Marco è più alto di Luca.

items.en: You are less tired than me.

items.it: È più facile leggere che scrivere.
items.en: It’s easier to read than to write.

items.it: Fa più caldo a Roma che a Milano.
items.en: It’s hotter in Rome than in Milan.

blocks.text: Equality: *come* or *quanto*: *Sono alto come te*.

The relative superlative (“the most”) = article + *più* + adjective + *di*: *Il Po è il fiume più lungo d’Italia*. The absolute superlative (“very”) adds *-issimo*: *bello → bellissimo*, *facile → facilissimo* — or uses *molto*: *molto bello*.
*meglio* and *peggio* are the adverbs (better / worse with verbs): *Lui canta meglio di me*. *migliore* is the adjective: *un lavoro migliore*.

exercises.en: My sister is as tall as me.
This pizza is better than that one.
You speak Italian better than me.
exercises.why: With a verb you need the adverb *meglio*.

exercises.it: È il ragazzo più simpatico ___ classe.
exercises.en: He is the nicest boy in the class.

exercises.sentence: Il Po è il fiume più lungo d’Italia
exercises.en: The Po is the longest river in Italy.

blocks.text: *che* (who, which, that) is the basic relative pronoun for subjects and direct objects. It never changes and is never left out, unlike English “that”.

items.it: Il ragazzo che parla è mio cugino.
items.en: The boy who is speaking is my cousin.

items.it: Il libro che leggo è bello.
items.en: The book (that) I’m reading is good.

blocks.text: After a preposition use *cui*: *la persona con cui lavoro* (the person I work with), *la città in cui vivo* (the city I live in), *il motivo per cui…* (the reason why…).
*il cui, la cui, i cui, le cui* = “whose”; the article agrees with the thing owned: *lo scrittore il cui libro…*, *la ragazza i cui genitori…*
*il quale, la quale, i quali, le quali* can replace *che* or *cui* in formal style: *la persona con la quale lavoro*.
*chi* means “the person who / whoever” and takes a singular verb: *Chi studia impara* (Whoever studies learns).

exercises.it: La donna ___ abita qui è francese.
exercises.en: The woman who lives here is French.

exercises.it: Il film ___ ho visto era noioso.
exercises.en: The film I saw was boring.
exercises.why: Direct object → *che* (it can’t be left out).

exercises.it: Questo è l’amico con ___ vado in vacanza.
exercises.en: This is the friend I’m going on holiday with.

exercises.it: La città in ___ sono nato è piccola.
exercises.en: The town I was born in is small.

exercises.it: Non capisco il motivo per ___ è arrabbiato.
exercises.en: I don’t understand why he is angry.
exercises.why: *il motivo per cui* = the reason why.

exercises.it: È una scrittrice ___ libri sono famosi.
exercises.en: She is a writer whose books are famous.

exercises.sentence: Ecco la ragazza di cui ti ho parlato
exercises.en: Here’s the girl I told you about.

blocks.text: The *congiuntivo* is used after *che* when the main verb expresses an opinion, doubt, wish, fear, or emotion: *penso che, credo che, voglio che, spero che, ho paura che, sono contento che*. It also follows *è importante / è necessario / è possibile che* and *benché, affinché, prima che*.
The three singular forms are identical, so the subject pronoun is often kept for clarity: *Penso che lui parta domani*.
If both verbs have the same subject, use *di* + infinitive instead: *Penso di partire* (I think I’ll leave), not *Penso che io parta*.

exercises.en: I want you to come with me.
I’m afraid it’ll start to rain.
We need to leave at once.

title: Stare + gerund
summary: I am doing it right now

blocks.text: The gerund ends in *-ando* (*-are* verbs) or *-endo* (*-ere* and *-ire* verbs): *parlare → parlando*, *leggere → leggendo*, *dormire → dormendo*. Irregular: *fare → facendo*, *dire → dicendo*, *bere → bevendo*.

*stare* + gerund stresses that something is happening right now: *Sto mangiando* = I’m eating (at this moment). It is used less than English “-ing”: for general or future actions Italian uses the simple present.

items.en: We were sleeping when you called.

blocks.text: *stare per* + infinitive = to be about to: *Sto per uscire* (I’m about to go out).
The gerund alone can mean “while / by doing”: *Camminando ho visto Anna* (While walking I saw Anna). Pronouns attach to it: *guardandolo*.

exercises.it: Ieri sera ___ la TV quando è andata via la luce.
exercises.en: Last night we were watching TV when the power went out.
The train is about to leave.
exercises.why: *stare per* + infinitive = to be about to.

exercises.en: I’m about to leave the house.

blocks.text: The *trapassato prossimo* = “had done”: an action that happened before another past action. Form: *imperfetto* of *avere / essere* + past participle. The choice of auxiliary and the agreement follow the *passato prossimo* rules.

items.it: Quando sono arrivato, il film era già cominciato.
items.en: When I arrived, the film had already started.

items.it: Non avevo mai visto il mare.
items.en: I had never seen the sea.

items.it: Mi ha detto che aveva perso le chiavi.
items.en: He told me he had lost his keys.

exercises.en: When we arrived, the train had already left.

exercises.it: Non ___ un film così bello. (vedere, io)
exercises.en: I had never seen such a good film.

exercises.it: Anna mi ha detto che ___ la torta. (fare)
exercises.en: Anna told me she had made the cake.
The girls had already gone out.
We were tired because we had slept little.
He knew that I had already eaten.
exercises.why: Earlier action reported in the past → *trapassato*: *avevo già mangiato*.

exercises.en: I had already finished my homework.

title: Imperfect and past subjunctive
summary: *pensavo che fosse…, penso che sia stato…*

blocks.text: The *congiuntivo imperfetto* is used when the main verb is in a past tense (or the conditional) and the two actions happen at the same time: *Pensavo che fosse vero* (I thought it was true).
Irregular: *essere → fossi*, *fare → facessi*, *dire → dicessi*, *bere → bevessi*, *dare → dessi*, *stare → stessi*.

The *congiuntivo passato* (present subjunctive of *avere / essere* + participle) is for an earlier action after a present main verb: *Penso che sia partito* (I think he has left). After a past main verb, the earlier action takes the *congiuntivo trapassato* (*avessi / fossi* + participle): *Pensavo che fosse partito* (I thought he had left).
*vorrei che* (I’d like) is always followed by the imperfect subjunctive: *Vorrei che tu venissi*.

exercises.en: I’d like you to pay more attention.
I thought they lived in Rome.
I was hoping Marco would come.
I think Anna has already left.
exercises.why: Present main verb + earlier action → *congiuntivo passato*: *sia già partita*.

exercises.it: Non sapevo che voi ___ il film. (vedere)
exercises.en: I didn’t know you had already seen the film.
exercises.why: Past main verb + earlier action → *congiuntivo trapassato*: *aveste già visto*.

exercises.en: It was necessary for everyone to keep quiet.
I’d like you to stay here.

blocks.text: Italian “if” sentences (*periodo ipotetico*) come in three types:

items.en: If you come, I’ll introduce you to Anna.

items.it: Se fossi in te, non lo farei.
items.en: If I were you, I wouldn’t do it.

items.it: Se fossimo partiti prima, saremmo arrivati in tempo.
items.en: If we had left earlier, we would have arrived on time.

blocks.text: The past conditional = conditional of *avere / essere* + participle: *avrei fatto* (I would have done), *sarei andato* (I would have gone).
Never put the conditional after *se*. “If I would have…” in Italian is always *se avessi…*.

exercises.it: Se ___ bel tempo, andiamo al mare.
exercises.en: If the weather is nice, we’ll go to the seaside.
If I were rich, I would buy a boat.

exercises.it: Se avessi tempo, ___ un corso di cucina. (fare, io)
exercises.en: If I had time, I’d take a cooking class.

exercises.it: Se ___ prima, avresti preso il treno.
exercises.en: If you had left earlier, you would have caught the train.

exercises.it: Se lo avessi saputo, te lo ___.
exercises.en: If I had known, I would have told you.

exercises.it: Se ___ la lotteria, che cosa faresti?
exercises.en: If you won the lottery, what would you do?

exercises.why: *se* + imperfect subjunctive, main clause in the conditional.

exercises.sentence: Se fossi in te non partirei
exercises.en: If I were you, I wouldn’t leave.

title: The passive voice
summary: *è stato scritto, viene usato, si vende*

blocks.text: The passive = *essere* + past participle; the participle agrees with the subject. The agent is introduced by *da*: *Il libro è scritto da Calvino* (The book is written by Calvino).

items.it: Questi quadri sono stati dipinti nel Seicento.
items.en: These paintings were painted in the 17th century.

items.it: Il ponte fu costruito dai Romani.
items.en: The bridge was built by the Romans.

blocks.text: In simple tenses *venire* can replace *essere* and stresses the action: *La porta viene chiusa ogni sera* (The door is closed every evening).
*andare* + participle means “must be”: *Il modulo va compilato* (The form must be filled in).
The *si passivante* is very common for general statements: *si* + 3rd-person verb agreeing with the noun: *Qui si parla italiano*, *In Italia si mangiano molti spaghetti*.
Compound tenses of the passive have two participles: *è stata venduta* — both agree with the subject.

exercises.en: The book was written by Umberto Eco.
The street is cleaned every day.

exercises.it: In questo negozio ___ vendono libri usati.
exercises.en: Second-hand books are sold in this shop.
The shoes are made in Italy.

exercises.sentence: La Gioconda fu dipinta da Leonardo
exercises.en: The Mona Lisa was painted by Leonardo.

title: Passato remoto
summary: The past of stories and history

blocks.text: The *passato remoto* is a simple past tense for completed actions with no link to the present. It is the tense of history, literature and fairy tales. In everyday speech in northern and central Italy it is mostly replaced by the *passato prossimo*; in parts of the south it is still common in speech.
Many verbs are irregular, mainly in the *io*, *lui / lei* and *loro* forms:

items.en: Dante was born in Florence in 1265.

items.it: C’era una volta un re che ebbe tre figlie.
items.en: Once upon a time there was a king who had three daughters.

exercises.it: Quella sera io ___ un sogno strano. (fare)
exercises.en: That evening I had a strange dream.
When he saw her, he was happy.

exercises.it: Loro ___ a Roma per tre anni. (vivere)
exercises.en: They lived in Rome for three years.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Italian grammar: Combinations of clitics (impersonal si)
Wikipedia – Italian grammar: Past participle (impersonal si)

blocks.text: *si* + 3rd-person singular verb = a general subject, like English “one”, “people” or general “you”: *In Italia si mangia bene* (In Italy you eat well). *Come si dice …?* (How do you say …?)
With a reflexive verb, the impersonal *si* becomes *ci si*: *Ci si alza presto* (One gets up early).

Adjectives and participles that refer to the impersonal *si* are masculine plural: *Si è sempre stanchi la sera* (One is always tired in the evening). In compound tenses the auxiliary is *essere*: *Si è mangiato bene* (We ate well).
With *ne*, *si* becomes *se*: *Se ne parla molto* (People talk about it a lot).

items.it: Come si scrive il tuo nome?
items.en: How do you spell your name?

items.it: Quando si è giovani, si ha molta energia.
items.en: When you are young, you have a lot of energy.

exercises.en: How do you say “ciao” in English?
You eat well in this restaurant.
On Sundays one gets up late.

exercises.it: Quando si è ___, si dorme bene.
exercises.en: When you are tired, you sleep well.

exercises.it: Ieri sera ___ ballato fino a tardi.
exercises.en: Last night we danced until late.
People often talk about it on TV.

exercises.sentence: In Italia si beve molto caffè
exercises.en: In Italy people drink a lot of coffee.
